Author: @eatcarpet
Content:
This is an interesting take. The Japanese economy isn't really a "capitalist" system. The companies are always more or less always thought of as being half-private and half-public. The government and bureaucracy definitely won't be happy when they start to go "rogue" and going wayward from what the society expects of them. In that way, the bureaucracy is extremely controlling. But not only the bureaucracy, but the people generally follow this as well, and they will start to complain a lot if the company start going rogue and don't try to benefit the customers or even the society as a whole.

So these things don't actually "spontaneously" happen by some sort of an "inevitable" system or a structure, such as say, capitalism and privatization. But rather, there are constant push and pull that "guide" these "private" companies into certain directions. Japan is such a society that everybody keeps a check on everybody else. This is why it sometimes refer to itself as a "village society", where people are constantly checked, restrained and controlled by everybody else.

Author: @0rpheus
Content:
Why the U.S. Doesn’t Have Good Passenger or High-Speed Rail network (TL;DR: Follow the money because that’s how the USA works and to solve it make even more money or luck out in two other ways.)

Big Auto, Oil, and Airlines didn’t want the competition. Back when we could’ve built a great rail system (mid-1900s), companies like GM, Standard Oil, and later airline giants saw trains as a threat to their cash cows. So they pushed for cars and planes instead. Standard practice in the U.S., big mega corporations buy out/stifle any potential competition (look at the mag 7 of today and their behavior of the past 10-15 years and no I’m not saying its right or wrong I’m just saying that’s typical corporation behavior in the U.S.)

The government handed out free money to the Big Auto, Oil and Airlines. The 1956 Highway Act dumped $25B into building interstates (over $250B in today’s dollars), making it super easy to drive everywhere. Airports and airlines also got major public funding. Rail? Not so much. I don’t care how much better in the long run an idea is, most times if someone offers free money for something that they something will win out even if it sucks in the long term. Hard to fight “free” money.

Cars and planes = low risk, fast money. Well cars at least. Planes offered an extremely juicy return for the high risk. For private companies, trains are expensive and take decades to plan, build/execute and pay off. Cars and planes let them profit quickly without building much infrastructure themselves because taxpayers were already covering that part (haha taxpayers what suckers we are.) so cars and planes companies are basically getting all the money with very little risk to the private companies and with trains those companies (assuming they would enter the rail industry to try and compete) would have to have a lot of permanent liabilities open to a number of risks. I know which one I’m taking if I’m the CEO of one of these auto/oil/airline companies for the next 5-7 years.

They didn’t just ignore rail, they actively killed it like a good American capitalist should. Murica. GM, Firestone, and Standard Oil literally bought and tore out electric streetcar systems in tons of U.S. cities, replacing them with buses to force people into car culture. Look up the “Great American Streetcar Scandal.” Whoever says that didn’t happen, please let me have some of what you’re having. I’d like to have the ability to ignore some things to.

Also there was no political or existential/ weird identity risk to not building out rail unlike with the space, arms and political system race with the USSR post 1950s that drove a lot of innovation from a variety of fear based reasons.

Now we’re stuck. Because the economic policies we implemented/model we chose incentivized short-term profits and corporate interests to steer national transportation policy towards the those corporation's financial interests and it continues to do so. The USA missed the window to build a world-class rail network, that’s the truth so let’s get over it. Other countries went long-term. We went “what’ll make the most money next quarter? (or by the next four quarters...we have to give corporations credit for long term thinking too right?!)” And as for brightline, once those low hanging fruit options are done I have a feeling it will be a reaaaaaalllly long time before there’s another high speed rail or new rail option coming online in the USA. Can rail work and be profitable? yep. (everyone knows that you need an operational and real estate development model for a real cash cow...we aren't geniuses reinventing the wheel here. heck airlines are trying their hardest to take over airports and stop them from being public in any way for that same reason but will it happen in the usa? nope. why mess up an already great cash cow if you are one of those aforementioned industries? 


So if you're living in the USA your options are:

Find a way to move to Europe, Japan or China and gain residency or citizenship if rail/walkability (threw that in there because why not) is that important to you

Find a way to become such a cultural icon that you singlehandedly transform the transportation culture and therefore the transportation policy in the USA

Find a way to become so disgustingly wealthy that you can single handidly make your imagination become reality by throwing enough money at the problem.

Good luck

Author: @railwaymechanicalengineer4587
Content:
RAILWAYS NOT RAILROADS !!!
Since when did Japan have "Railroads". The Railway network in Japan was laid out (with British left hand drive amongst other things) as Railways by none other than Richard & Robert Trevithick, the Grandsons of the man who built the Worlds first Railway Steam Locomotive in Helston Cornwall in 1803. Indeed the first Railway Civil Engineer to arrive in Japan Edmund Morell who had just completed the surveying for the 3ft 6in Gauge New Zealand Railway network, had begun the planning in Japan, but had fallen out with the Japanese Authorities, for "dishonourable behaviour", so was replaced by the Trevithick Brothers who took the posts of Chief Railway Civil Engineer, & Chief Railway Mechanical Engineer. And between set up the formalative Japanese Imperial Railways (JIR).


The Trevithick's used of course already British standard Railway practices, including driving on the left, British "Absolute Block" signalling, British type high platforms, and initially imported British designed and built locomotives. Due to the delays (due to distance) of British built rolling stock. The Trevithick's quickly began the process of introducing Railway Workshops, to produce everything, including wagons, coaches and locomotives, in Japan. Only due to an economic crash in Japan, did the "door" open to allow Private companies to begin building Railways before the turn of the century in 1900. But most of these initial Railways were  taken over by the Government once the economic situation had resolved itself. Meaning "British Practices continued". 

Indeed in 1933 the Japanese Railways were attracted to a development in Britain, and sent a large Railway Investigative Party, to see the Southern Railway (UK) electrification of the first mainline railway, using the Worlds first Multi-Aspect (Colour light signals) that used the then revolutionary idea of "Continuous Track Circuits" to allow for safe operation of trains at TWO MINUTE INTERVALS ON EACH TRACK. Coupled to a "Regular interval timetable". This whole package resulted in the London to Brighton mainline train frequency being massively increased, with train mileage on this one route tripling overnight. Passenger number tripled with 18 months, as the new luxury Pullman Dining Car Electric Multiple Units (EMU's), also the first of their kind in the World, hugely increased the profits of the SR overnight. The Japanese were particularly interested in the new 4 Aspect signal methods for use in their cities. And the "Regular Interval Timetable" methods which was a revolution in itself drawing in many new customers who had never experienced railways previously. 

Indeed the Japanese Railways today still use that 1933, Multi aspect "Track Circuit Block" signalling method, enhanced to 5 aspects, to allow trains at just 90 second intervals on each track. Bullet train lines of course do NOT & CANNOT use trackside signalling, so use an in cab computer system based around "Moving Block" Rules. Meaning the signals appear constantly on the Drivers control desk.

Author: @vyli1
Content:
I think a huge reason why there even is profit to be had is the population size of Japan. There aren't that many countries in the world with Japan's level of population size, which means that the amount of passengers across the same distances will be much smaller, making it much less profitable. People mention in the comments the notoriously unreliable Deutsche Bahn. But the population of Germany is 84 million compared to Japans 124 million and while the area of Germany is smaller than Japan in total, the difference is rather small and the important part is, that Japan is almost a thin line of territory, while Germany's territory is wider. Also, german railway network needs to support international trains that cross borders and that's both personal trains and freight trains. When you look at the railway map of the rails operated by JR companies, it is a very simple network. Germany's network is bit more complex.

Japan has some unique features that allow rails to be successful there, but other countries do not have many of the advantages that allow Japan to turn railways into a profitable business.

I think there is a fundamental difference in philosophies: whereas lots of western governments see privatisation itself as the goal because 'private' is automatically equated to "efficient" both japan and China seem to have developed heavily controlled enclosed private sectors to boost development. So they seem to use privatisation not as a strict order, but as a tool to hypercharge, develop and streamline certain sectors. Another example is chinese car manufacturing. 
The common element in both examples is a strict government and public oversight andmost important: a clear goal BEYOND proffit. 
Japan: we want good service and that adapts to each of the regions' specifficities
China: we want to develop a competitive EV industry and reliable supply chains and manufacturing hubs for this sectors.

So as an analogy, privatisation would be like a shot of adrenaline supervised by a doctor.
In the west we are more like aimless junkies

Author: @DerClouder
Content:
It is SO weird Japan has almost exactly the same history with Finland when it comes to railways. Finnish State Railways(VR, Valtion Rautatiet) even has the same kind of logo! Not to mention the offshoot grocery vendors that used to serve passengers, but has since then spread to every corner of the country. In Finland, it is called R-Kioski(Railway kiosk) that was first owned by the VR, but later made into it's own company. Finland has only one subcidy under VR, called VR Cargo that deals with general freight, but there are multiple different freight train operators who, even though private companies, follow the VR control as to not create a conflict between passenger and cargo.

Cargo in general is transported by trucks these days, as it is in Japan, so only bulk cargo like gas and logs are transported via train these days so the main moneymaker for the VR is the passenger lines.

Author: @orinblank2056
Content:
It wasn't really elaborated on, but another key part of the rail network is having multiple different trains on the same route that have different stops. I lived in Osaka prefecture for a bit, in Hirakata, and having multiple lines makes things much easier. Each one has a different number of stops, so the local line will stop at every stop, the sub-express skips over a lot of the stops on the side towards Osaka, and the limited express only stops at the major stops. There are some other lines as well, but I rarely took them. Having those different lines makes everything way easier though. I could walk to the station near me and get on the local line, then ride 2 stops to Hirakata station and transfer over to the sub-express, and it is super easy. Comping back is even easier, because the sub-express is usually timed to a local line, meaning all you have to do is walk across the platform and right into another train.

Genuinely miss having good public transit to much now that I'm back in the US. For all the talk of freedom, I felt so much more free to do things in Japan, and it was way easier without having to deal with traffic. Plus, since everybody rides the train nobody really goes anywhere after the trains stop at midnight. I could sit in the park, in the middle of the city, and part of the 10th largest metropolitan area on earth, and it would be totally quiet. The noise was comparable to my 2000 person hometown in the US, it was amazing

Author: @GreenSpacebug
Content:
0:35

While the Shinkansen is really safe, Sam's statement here is incorrect. There have been two derailments in the Shinkansen's operation history. One in 2004 on the Joetsu Shinkansen during the Chuetsu earthquakes, the other in 2013, on the Akita Shinkansen due to blizzard conditions. Both yielded no fatalities. 

The Shinkansen's safety history is high (no fatalities due to derailments or collisions), but the no fatalities statement is also false. There have been multiple fatalities on the train caused by passengers (multiple suicides, one passenger lit himself on fire and killed another, etc.), and one fatality caused by the train itself. 

In 1995, at Mishima Station, a 17 year old schoolboy was unfortunately dragged along the train, as his finger was caught as the doors closed (he was not fully boarded yet). The Shinkansen doors, when closed, enact an airtight seal, so the student was killed as he was unable to remove himself while the train moved. It was found that the teen's finger diameter was smaller than the diameter used by a device in the door to detect foreign objects to prevent it from closing. As a result, JR West had to make changes to the train so that the doors would only enact an air tight seal once the speed reached 30 kph.

Author: @Tinil0
Content:
Another factor that isn't talked about here, partially because not much time was spent on the idea of trying to export the lessons from Japan in rail privatization in other countries which is totally fair, is that capitalism (despite frequent accusations) isn't one single way of doing things and the various interests and cultural aspects of the society determine how things function.  In Japan, capitalism is far, far, FAR more long-term thinking when it comes to profit than in a place like the United States for instance.  Companies can and have ran in the red continuously for literally decades, all in the promise of future profitability.  Where in the US everything is focused on IMMEDIATE profit at all costs, in Japan there is much more understanding among both investors and corporate executives that building long term profit is far better than extracting as much value as fast as possible.  Companies are built to capitalize on markets that may not even exist and receive patience and support in investment from banks and individuals without any need to turn it around in the next quarter.

(Tangentially and off-topic, it is exceedingly frustrating when people ignorantly assume that the way capitalism works in the US is fundamentally the way capitalism HAS to work or that it's the "true" form of capitalism.  It is highly flawed in ways that can absolutely be fixed if there was a concerted effort, but the damage the rich have done have turned people into such black and white thinkers they can't even conceive of the system working in a long term way, they think "short term profit over all else" is what defines the system)

Author: @avikarpik
Content:
I've been to Japan twice (8 weeks total) and Japanese trains are backpacker's wet dream. I planned my route, checked prices for individual trains, then I bought JR Pass. Transport between 4 cities already paid for the pass, when I had 6 or 7 cities on my planned list. Not included in my price calculations to make JR Pass money-efficient, I hopped locally through so many trains/lines for side trips - JR Pass covers way more than just Shinkansen lines! When I was in Osaka, I literally hopped on a 15 min train to check out if I want to go to Kobe and stay there for a couple days... From my hostel to Chinatown in Kobe, it took 25 mins. This is as much it takes me to get to work where I live, yet I live and work in the same city! So no wonder lots of people in Japan commute to work to towns that are 100-150kms away. 

JR Pass even paid for some JR-owned buses to tourist destinations. Buses go where JR trains can't, they are extension of some train lines - coordinated and waiting at the train station to pick up people and go immediately after you disembark the train. Travel speed and train frequency are perfect, though some tourist destinations have limited departures but they are matched to 'day trip' standard - leave at 8am, come back at 5pm for example. 

The only hassle is that Google Maps DO NOT understand connections in many places. Tokyo is mostly all right but many other cities are not working as expected on Google Maps. The moment journey consists of 3 trains with 1 min change, Google might suggest the next train, adding wait time when there should be none. So I highly suggest Japan Travel app (from Japan National Tourism Organization) as it has a deeper understanding of those seemingly tight connections. And those connections aren't that tight, even slow moving grandma can move from one side of the platform to the other side in 60s, the distance is 5-6m and doors are usually aligned. But you have to be ready at the door before you arrive to the station, and I've seen some tourists unaware how short the stops are lol.

Author: @ichifish
Content:
Good video, but the conclusion is not correct. The success of the train companies is only partially related to the division of JR and public support. The primary reason is the Japan's geography and culture align perfectly with public transportation. There's no way I'd commute daily on a jam-packed train in any American city. It would be miserable. Here I ride about 30 minutes in a reasonably crowded (shoulder to shoulder) train and it's a pleasure. 

Japan is clean to the point of sterility. Sure, rail companies put effort into keeping their trains and stations clean - I can see my reflection on the side of the train I take every day and the toilets are not only spotless but full of new tech - but PEOPLE here are clean and respectful about keeping public spaces clean. I can't understate how far this goes to make the ride better, and I'm not what you'd call a clean person myself. Passengers are quiet and keep to themselves. Boring by American standards - Japanese people don't generally make small talk with strangers - but absolutely the best attitude for getting a lot of people to ride peacefully on the train.

Japanese culture highly values following rules and minimizing risks, which makes running railways easier. 

Yes, Japan is a car country in the sense that a surprisingly high number of people own cars, but a lot of those cars sit in the driveway until the weekend. There's also a lot of company vehicles purchased as a write-off. Although insurance is reasonable, driving in Japan is expensive. I paid about $160 in tolls driving four hours away this weekend (round trip). There's also a lot of traffic.

And don't downplay the importance of population density. 90% of the population lives in urban or dense urban environments.

Author: @archie4oz
Content:
0:10 minor correction, should be 8hrs and 4hrs respectively.

One other aspect that Sam overlooked is what is known as the 3rd pillar of the Japanese Rail model and that's the financial leg. Nowadays most transit agencies outsource the fare capture infrastructure to 3rd parties, however the JR companies largely own, operate, and develop their own fare capture infrastructure. This allows them a lot more freedom in creating financial instruments that can piggy back off of it.

Using JR East as an example, with the development of Suica, they slowly built a customer base essentially carrying an electronic stored-value e-money purse. That means they're earning interest on the float of the stored-value (when you consider there's 95+ million physical and mobile Suica cards in circulation it adds up!). They have more fine-grained control over custom fare options to support promotions to drive more traffic. They have point system (JRE Point) for incentives to drive customer retention. They have their own bank (JRE Bank) now, and issue credit cards (VIEW Card) that integrate with their transit IC. The transit ICs acceptance as digital currency has grown so that all sorts of businesses around the city accept it, means you're getting transaction revenue from your rail customers well outside the just the station and fare capture at the gate.

Author: @nbnb7263
Content:
Privatization of the Japanese National Railways certainly contributed to the recovery of the railway business, but at the same time it encouraged fierce competition among JR companies to improve management and services.

This obsession led JR companies (especially JR West) to increase the number of trains and operate at high speeds while cutting staff and wages, which eventually led to serious accidents such as ”The Amagasaki derailment(「JR福知山線脱線事故」"JR Fukuchiyama Line derailment")”.

The situation is said to be improving now, but there is criticism that the workload of railway employees throughout the industry is still very heavy.

In addition, the management situation of many local railways continues to deteriorate due to population decline, concentration in cities, and the decline of local industries, and when damaged by earthquakes or storms, there are many cases where they are abolished because there is no prospect of recovery. (Especially in Hokkaido)

(I am Japanese and I used a translation software to write this, so I apologize if it sounds unnatural.)

Author: @kFY514
Content:
Coming from Europe, what astonished me the most about Japanese railways is the strict organization into _lines._ Of course every rail system has lines, but in Japan they are presented front and center to the end customer, compared to how they are mostly hidden from European rail customers. You don't hop onto a "train to Osaka", you take the Tōkaidō Shinkansen (note that "shinkansen" literally means "New Main Line"), or the older Tōkaidō Line. Basically every train route in Japan, including Shinkansen, operates like a metro line - it's a connection between end stations that operates more or less independently from the rest of the network.

I actually experienced the rare instance of delays on Japanese rail - service on one of the lines was suspended due to trespassing. When the situation was handled, the service resumed - but that didn't cause a ton of unrelated trains to be delayed - services were only suspended _on that given line._ This organization means that  Japanese travelers need transfers more often, but a single failure doesn't ripple over the entire network too much, and a nicely integrated ticket system means that the pain of transferring is reduced to a minimum.

It is a very different way of traveling compared to what we're used to in Europe, especially if we're talking about the "regular" lines (and not the Shinkansen). It feels like taking a metro system that spans the entire country rather than a traditional intercity railway - the lines tend to be relatively short but run with very high frequencies. And I need to say that I actually like the Japanese system, it feels much more flexible and reliable.

Author: @yohannessulistyo4025
Content:
Not mentioned, but very important to success of this model across Asia:
- Government-private synergy, in a way that a lot of private players do perform 'public service'. The difference with the west is that, they don't take profits or just take reasonable amounts of it. Even non railway real estate owners willingly drill a tunnel to gain direct access to a subway system from their property
- Private-private synergy, while competing, they also work together and share facilities and support each other, some private operators let others use their tracks or use their stations
It works in Asia, because politics are politics, and business are business. "Democracy" like Japan and Singapore are basically one-party system with voting rituals to appease their western audiences and western media scrutiny. Businesses can stick to their long term planning and trust the commitment from the stable government. It is not like politicians could dominate the spectacle, override experts, and tell their gullible self-righteous voters that their heroic figure just "saved tax payer's money" by cancelling HSR2 or "secured our future" by developing a new transit line - only to be wasted by the next voting cycle winner.
There are always risks that one day those powerful private players could turn into government-controlling oligarchs. For now, east Asian Confucian society structure prevented that - with the public being very wary of it and could immediately tap into their world-renowned toxic cancel culture that could drive any corrupt politicians or even untouchable oligarchs to commit suicide. But with ever more westernisation of our society, that worships individual success and wealthy individuals, the social control will eventually fade one day, and Asia will fail because of it.

Author: @giutyutgiuty
Content: JR Central derives 92% of its transportation revenue from the Tōkaidō Shinkansen, making it extremely profitable. For special reasons, the company controls the area from Tokyo, Shinagawa, and Shin-Yokohama to Kyoto and Shin-Osaka. For example, while the conventional train lines at Tokyo Station are operated by JR East, the Shinkansen platforms are under the jurisdiction of JR Central. The Shinkansen has not increased its speed, as further improvements in speed would be meaningless due to the lack of competition from other modes of domestic transportation, such as airplanes. On the other hand, JR Hokkaido and JR Shikoku are operating at a loss, unable to break even. Currently, the government’s special corporation is the 100% shareholder, and there is no prospect of these companies being listed on the stock market.

Author: @GlenMcCabe
Content:
As someone who lived in Japan for 9 years and used both the transit system and drove a lot, this is a nice summary. It perhaps underplays the role of road traffic - there are plenty of suburban, exurban and rural areas without much or any rail service - but overall you've captured the essence of the rail system there. Two things which needed to be discussed more IMHO:
1. Where the debts of the JNR came from. Yes, the JNR focused on train ops and missed many revenue opportunities. But politics also drive it to build lines in rural areas which would never justify a line and the rugged terrain meant very high construction costs. A very few of them successfully opened as 'third sector ' (local government + private business) lines, such as the Hokuhoku Line and Chizu Line which offered/offer express through service, but many lost money and were closed before privatisation or were abandoned partly built.
2 Closing unprofitable lines has been streamlined by the regional mobility act (paraphrase name) of a couple of years ago. There is a big wave of closures coming, particularly in the JR West area. The Geibi Line is just the most egregious example of an unprofitable line, plenty more are on the chopping block.

Author: @NerdX151
Content: As someone who lives in Japan, there is only one thing that I really dislike about the Japanese railway system: The lack of an affordable InterCity system. Coming from Europe, I am used to having 3 modes of transportation when it comes to trains: Local trains that cover short distances between regional centers and surroundings areas, InterCity trains that link the major cities with only a few stops, and Highspeed Trains that link major cities faster at a higher ticket cost. In Japan, if I want to travel directly between Osaka and Tokyo I have only two options. I either pay a very expensive Shinkansen ticket or I take a highway bus which takes almost half a day. Before privatization you could still travel between Tokyo and Osaka on a regular train. The journey took around 6 hours on the Tokaido Mainline which was perfectly acceptable, but today you will need to do 5 to 6 transfers between different private companies, meaning that the journey takes almost the same time as the highway bus, despite having modern tracks all the way, which accept speeds up to 140 km/h. There is absolutely a market for an InterCity model. People here would gladly pay less to travel on a direct comfortable train between Tokyo and Osaka, but its impossible because of the private companies and their interests on their part of the mainline.

Author: @トロント-g8j
Content:
I'm Japanese. As mentioned in this video, one major reason why the three JR companies on Honshu were able to operate independently is that Japan had railway lines managed by private companies from the beginning. To distinguish them from JNR and JR, these private railways are referred to as "Shitetsu" in Japan.

Because of this, each JR company was able to follow the successful business practices of Shitetsu, and they have generally been successful in metropolitan areas where profitability is easier to achieve. A similar privatization process was carried out for the Teito Rapid Transit Authority (Tokyo National Subway), which was reborn as "Tokyo Metro" and is now listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

On the other hand, there are voices arguing that public transportation should not be treated as a for-profit business but rather as a basic human right. Some believe that, like in Europe, the public sector should provide more support and maintain operations even if they run at a loss. This sentiment is particularly strong in rural areas, where many railway lines were transferred to local public entities when JNR was privatized.

Additionally, when new Shinkansen lines open, many of the parallel conventional railway lines are transferred to semi-public companies, in which local public entities also invest.

In relation to this, Germany’s Stadtbahn and the concept of light rail in the United States have been introduced to Japan as a means of alleviating traffic congestion and reducing car dependency. As a result, the value of publicly managed tram systems has been reevaluated, leading to an increase in the adoption of European-style low-floor vehicles. Furthermore, in 2023, a new light rail system was completed in Utsunomiya (Tochigi Prefecture), near Tokyo, and its popularity has become a significant topic in the field of regional transportation.

Author: @shehranazim4784
Content:
Speaking as a Brit living in Japan for almost 6 years, this video does a good job of showing off just how great the train system is here. One point that wasn't brought up, especially with respect to the car situation here, is that pretty much all the expressways are toll roads here in Japan, so if you want to drive anywhere quick, you're paying a hefty premium.

In the UK, it's not uncommon for people to just drive everywhere (I personally did the London-Leeds run every weekend for a long while) because it's cheaper than getting the train, for not that much more time (3 hours vs 2). I know the US is far worse with its reliance on cars, to the point where my American friends and colleagues don't even bat an eyelid at the prospect of an 11 hour drive.

Here in Japan, you'll pretty much end up paying about the same amount as a Shinkansen ticket (11,000 JPY) in tolls (8,000 JPY) and fuel costs (3,000 JPY) for the equivalent 200 mile Nagoya to Tokyo run, only for it to take 3x as long. Although I love driving and road trips, I basically just stick to using my car within the prefecture, or for journeys to areas that aren't served by the Shinkansen. Hell, I've even trained it to far flung places and just rented a car for the weekend because it's cheaper and easier than driving there.

The "earthquake" produced by the investigation report, which did not only concern the accident, caused all private companies and JR to be "investigated" by the Japanese state, and most of the failures of JR-west were found in all companies.

Nowadays, companies are offering "lighter" frequencies and are more tolerant of delays, because there are often some, particularly on suburban trains, and security systems have been installed on all trains, even the older ones.

Now the main problem of these companies is the staff... the population is aging, the companies are trying to compensate for the lack of employees mainly through automation, as well as the withdrawal of train chief.

As for the closure of unprofitable lines, it has been accelerating for 5 years, very often replaced by bus lines.

The bus network throughout Japan is already at the top echelon because the job is very poorly paid.

Author: @abarratt8869
Content:
A big part of the recovery is reliability. And reliability of Japanese rail is down to one thing, and one thing only. They firmly believe in and fully understand the importance of frequent inspection for faults. 

Consider the Shinkansen. There's essentially zero faults on any of the Shinkansen lines. There's a track survey train - called Dr Yellow - that is run (I think) every other day, and there's gangs of maintenance crew on hand to fix any discovered issues. The entire line is surveyed so frequently that faults barely have time to manifest before they're fixed, and never ever become major equipment failures. 

And when a Shinkansen gets to a terminal station it's pounced on by an maintenance team (they've got their own platform underneath the passenger platform) who look at the train. Those train sets probably get looked at several times a day, each. 

By looking at their infrastructure so regularly, and addressing any imperfection immediately, they're probably doing less actual fixing in total than anyone else. 

And if the track, trains, and signalling are in perfect working order, it becomes possible to run a service timetable very accurately. Which means your timetabling can become very ambitious with connection times (like, 30 seconds). Which means people really can do lots of complex journeys with minimal waiting time. Which makes the rail option highly appealing.

All in all, it's a solid lesson in what you can achieve if you put enough of the right sort of manpower doing things proactively, instead of reactively.

Content:

THIS! 

People often get into arguments, government service vs private corporations. People who favour more government services will point to how lots of attempts to privatize government services have not gone so well. They are correct! But the reason they don't go so well, is because when these services are privatized, they're not restructured for a private market. They end up forming de-facto monopolies, just, run by someone else instead of the government. 

The key to private industry being successful is in a) flexibility of operations and structure; and b) competition. If you take a large bureaucratic system, with no flexibility, and give it to one single private operator, with no competition, it's going to go poorly. Privatization is (at least in my opinion) generally good, but it's not a magic wand. You need to be very thoughtful and deliberate about how, specifically, you implement it, if you want to see benefits

Author: @91Durktheturk
Content:
I'm not so sure if you can say that Japanese Railway companies are profitable. The nationalised operator basically went bust under the weight of the colossal debt incurred for Shinkansen construction at the end of the 1980s. This debt has never been paid off and went into the books of the Japanese government, which has a gigantic debt to GDP ratio as a result. 

I think for this reason, you cannot really conclude that the Shinkansen are a success. However, if you look at the regional and commuter railways in Japan, I think any railway company around the world should go and learn from them. They did not focus on increasing line speeds, but on segregating flows to avoid conflicting movements at interchange stations by building dive-unders, flyovers etc to avoid trains being clogged up at flat junctions. This has massively increased line capacity, enabling them to run a very high frequency service, which attracts a lot of demand. If you then ensure that interchanges between lines are convenient, through cross-platform interchanges, you win even more. The Dutch Railways learned actually copied this strategy from the 1970s onwards, which has been very successful. In NL, you will not find very fast trains, but lots of dive-unders and flyovers near the important stations to segregate flow and to maximise train throughput. 

In my view this is the real reason why Japanese trains win. It is not the Shinkansen, it is the commuter and regional railways of Japan that lead the way and show how things can be done. Get the most out of your existing infrastructure. And then you can run trains at a profit.

Sadly, Tokaido Shinkansen has been saturated for years. To prevent overcrowding, nowadays all seats on Nozomi (the fastest service) are reserved during the following:

1) New year period

3) The period in mid-August called “お盆”, where people go back to hometown to visit their ancestors’ graves

That’s why both the maglev Chuo Shinkansen, together with the final phase of Hokuriku Shinkansen need to be completed ASAP.

Author: @BellePullman
Content: In Japan in 1987, there was a phenomenally successful Arena tour of the musical "Starlight Express", about a child's toy train set coming to life in his dream for a massive championship race.  The timing is such a coincidence that the country was going through such upheaval in its rail system at the time - trains must have been in the news, in the conscious, every day, and then the most spectacular arena tour of singing, dancing, roller skating trains? It must have helped!  The production was a UK/US import to Japan, the intention was the Japanese dates would be like an "out of town try-out" for the following Australian dates - it turned out the show was far more popular in Japan, and they returned a couple years later.  The pure glorious 1980s excess didn't survive beyond 1990, sadly.

Author: @wclifton968gameplaystutorials
Content:
Japanese Railways: Vertically integrated transport companies, mostly privately owned, operates both Railway, and Bus service, and has large property holdings
GB Railways (England, Scotland & Wales): It is illegal to vertically operate a transport company with large property holdings; Train Operating Companies (TOC) do not own all stations, do not own tracks, any changes must be approved by the Department for Transport, And don't even think about the TOC's parent company operating bus service in the same region as the TOC (there will be a 'Competition Commission' investigation); Most TOCs are State-Owned, mostly by the UK Government's DfT OLR, but some by other countries, such as c2c being owned by FS Trenitalia (Italian state-owned Railway company) Deutsche Bahn has sold Arriva in 2024 to an American company, so does not count).

Author: @GT670DN
Content: Most important factor is, that japanese railways are integrated companies. Network and operations are controlled by the very same entity. Contract boundaries between entities always makes stuff harder to do.
